content: Brugmansia is a genus of six species of flowering plants belonging to the family Solanaceae. These plants are native to subtropical regions of South America, specifically along the Andes from Colombia to northern Chile, as well as southeastern Brazil. Commonly referred to as Angel's Trumpets, they share this name with the closely related genus Datura. However, Brugmansia differs from Datura in several key ways: Brugmansia species are perennial and woody, whereas Datura species are herbaceous. Additionally, Brugmansia flowers are pendulous (hanging downward), unlike the erect flowers of Datura. Brugmansia plants are large shrubs or small trees, typically growing to heights of 3 to 11 meters. Their bark is tan-colored and slightly rough in texture. The leaves are alternately arranged, generally large, measuring 10–30 cm in length and 4–18 cm in width. The leaf margins may be entire or coarsely toothed, and the leaves are covered with fine hairs. The name Angel's Trumpet refers to the plant's large, dramatic, trumpet-shaped flowers, which are pendulous in orientation. These flowers can range in size from 14 to 50 cm in length and 10 to 35 cm in diameter at their widest point. They come in a variety of colors, including white, yellow, pink, orange, and red. The flowers emit a delicate, pleasant fragrance with light, lemony overtones, which is most noticeable in the early evening. The six species of Brugmansia are as follows: Brugmansia arborea: Found in the Andes, from Ecuador to northern Chile. Brugmansia aurea: Native to the Andes, from Colombia to Ecuador. Brugmansia sanguinea: Found in the Andes, from Colombia to Peru and Bolivia. Brugmansia suaveolens: Native to southeastern Brazil, extending westward to Bolivia and Peru. Brugmansia versicolor: Found in Ecuador. Brugmansia vulcanicola: Native to Colombia. Cultivation Brugmansia plants are relatively easy to cultivate in moist, fertile, well-drained soil. They thrive in full sun to partial shade and are best suited to frost-free climates. In warm climates, they begin flowering in mid to late spring and continue to bloom into the fall, often extending as late as early winter under favorable conditions. In regions with cool winters, outdoor plants require protection, although their roots are hardy and can resprout in April or May. Species from higher elevations, such as B. sanguinea and B. vulcanicola, prefer moderate temperatures and cool nights. These species may not flower well in very hot conditions. Most Brugmansia species can be propagated easily by rooting 10–20 cm cuttings taken from the ends of branches during the summer. Numerous hybrids and cultivars have been developed for ornamental purposes. For example: B. × candida is a hybrid between B. aurea and B. versicolor. B. × insignis is a hybrid between B. suaveolens and B. versicolor. Some cultivars of B. × candida produce flowers in shades of white, yellow, pale orange, or pink. B. × insignis produces flowers in white or peach tones. The flowers of B. versicolor start as white and gradually turn salmon pink. Additionally, there are cultivars with double flowers and some with variegated leaves. Uses All parts of Brugmansia are highly toxic, similar to the related genus Datura. The plant contains tropane alkaloids, including scopolamine and atropine, which can cause severe intoxication. Despite its toxicity, Brugmansia is sometimes ingested for recreational or shamanic purposes due to its psychoactive properties. However, the potency of the toxic compounds in the plant is highly variable, making the degree of intoxication unpredictable and potentially fatal. Ritualized consumption of Brugmansia is an important aspect of shamanic practices among various Indigenous peoples of western Amazonia, such as the Jivaroan-speaking groups. It also plays a central role in the cosmology and shamanic traditions of the Urarina people of Loreto, Peru. Additional Information Brugmansia is recognized as an official International Cultivar Registration Authority, as designated in the 2004 edition of the International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants.
